title: Autonomous Ocean Profiling Robot for Climate Monitoring
text:
A picture of our final robot build.
  

  
    All spring semester sophomore engineers at Harvey Mudd undergo a rigorous lab-based class called E80, or Experimental Engineering. In the latter half of this class, students work in teams to develop a fully autonomous underwater robot that measures a phenomenon of their choice with a limit of $50 to purchase sensors. At the end of the class, the robot is deployed at Dana Point Beach, a harbor in the suburbs of Los Angeles.

    Our team chose to measure pressure, temperature, and ultraviolet light intensity as a function of depth in marine environments — phenomena directly tied to ocean health and climate monitoring. With a tight budget and real deployment conditions, every engineering decision carried weight.

    I led the electrical system design, implementing 3 analog circuits with three unique electrical interfaces: voltage-to-voltage, current-to-voltage, and resistance-to-voltage. Each sensor system — UV, pressure, and temperature — was engineered using a unity-gain buffer and inverting gain amplifier to tailor sensor output to a specific range, enhancing data resolution and preventing data clipping on the Teensy 4.0.

    Calibration was one of the most technically demanding aspects of the project. I developed protocols that accounted for noise, sensor non-linearity, and degradation — ensuring robust and accurate measurements across diverse underwater conditions. On the mechanical side, I helped design and fabricate a system that maintained neutral buoyancy in saltwater while minimizing axial tilt, improving stability during data collection.
To control the robot autonomously, I developed a C++ algorithm for dynamic depth control, enabling the robot to reach and maintain designated waypoints at various depths. Once the data was collected, I developed MATLAB scripts to process the output and generate clear, interpretable graphs of temperature and UV intensity as a function of depth — aiding data analysis and decision-making for climate monitoring.

GENERAL MOTORS —  Autonomous Robotics Center Manufacturing Engineering Intern
This past summer, I interned at General Motors’ within the department of General Assembly and Autonomous Robtoics Center Division in Burton, Michigan as a Manufacturing Engineering Intern. I was directly on the floor of a live processing plant, supporting the launch and integration of an Automated Storage and Retrieval System (ASRS) — a large-scale automation initiative aimed at transforming how materials are stored, retrieved, and delivered across production departments.
My role placed me at the intersection of engineering and operations, where I worked alongside cross-functional teams to redesign material-handling workflows, analyze production data, and develop workstation concepts that would support the seamless transition to a more automated environment.
I also had the privilege of developing and earning a Green Belt in Design for Six Sigma (DFSS) — a certification that has fundamentally shaped how I approach engineering problems. DFSS trained me to minimize variation and bias in process design, allowing me to build fine-tuned solutions that are statistically validated.

DASION — Software Engineer & ML Intern
This past summer, I interned at Dasion as a Software Engineer and Machine Learning Intern based in Claremont, California. Dasion is a data-driven company focused on leveraging machine learning to support medical and behavioral research. My role placed me at the intersection of software engineering and applied machine learning, where I worked on developing tools to support emotion recognition in children using medical imaging data.
Working on a project with real clinical implications pushed me to think carefully about model selection, data quality, and the downstream impact of engineering decisions. Every preprocessing step, every architecture choice, and every evaluation metric carried weight — because the end users were researchers and practitioners working with vulnerable populations.
One of the most exciting aspects of this internship was building an emotion-based music recommender using the Spotify API — a creative application that connected the emotional state detected by our models to curated playlists, demonstrating the real-world potential of the system beyond clinical settings.

HARVEY MUDD COLLEGE — Machine Shop Proctor
The Harvey Mudd Machine Shop serves as a creative space for the 7 Claremont Colleges, welcoming people from all different backgrounds in machining to work on personal projects, class projects, and team projects — allowing for the full spectrum of the creative space to come to life. The shop features both a wooden shop and a metal shop, each equipped with a variety of tools that support everything from early-stage prototyping to precision manufacturing.
As a Machine Shop Proctor, my role is to guide new and existing users on safe practices while assisting with project development for classes. This means being present on the floor, understanding what each person is trying to build, and helping them navigate the right tools, techniques, and processes to get there — safely and effectively.
Beyond day-to-day guidance, I participate in weekly trainings that continuously build my knowledge of machining, tooling, and manufacturing processes. These sessions have deepened my understanding of the machines I work with and made me a more effective resource for the students and makers who rely on the shop.
I also play a direct role in supporting engineering courses at Harvey Mudd, including Introduction to Engineering Design and Manufacturing and Mechanical Design, where I guide students through reading and following process routers and technical drawings to manufacture components to specification — skills that form the foundation of any engineering career.

title: Flexible Measuring Laser
text:
The Flexible Measuring Laser system.
  

  
    

    Users of the Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) are required to manually estimate the height of their mounted samples before placing them inside the microscope chamber. This estimation — typically done by visually comparing the sample against a ruler — is inherently inconsistent and prone to error. Inaccurate height inputs can lead to collisions inside the chamber, causing damage to sensitive detectors or degrading microscope performance.

    The client requested a height measurement solution that would allow trained users to quickly, safely, and accurately determine the maximum sample height for any standard SEM sample holder. The solution needed to accommodate all existing holder bases with at most a 10 cm radius, provide readout tolerances within 0.5 mm, and critically — make no contact with the top surface of the sample, which is coated in a conductive layer only nanometers thick that could be irreparably damaged by even the lightest touch.
To meet these requirements, I designed a precision rack and pinion Z-axis measurement system integrated with a laser and photosensor, paired with a slew bearing for radial motion. This allowed the system to sweep around the sample and detect its tallest point without ever making contact. The entire measurement process was designed to be completed in under two minutes by a trained non-specialist user.
Material selection was a critical part of the design process. Through a full fatigue and material analysis, I selected PLA for its scalability and ease of use in 3D printing — ensuring the device would remain accurate, durable, and easily replicable over its lifetime. The final design prevents $1000+ in potential equipment damage from improper sample height inputs.

title: Machinist’s Hammer
text:
The finished machinist's hammer.
  

  
    Precision machining is a fundamental skill in mechanical engineering, requiring the ability to read and interpret technical drawings and manufacture components to tight tolerances. This project was motivated by the need to develop hands-on machining skills using industry-standard equipment and processes.

    The goal was to manufacture a fully functional machinist hammer from raw materials including clear oak, AISI 1015 steel, AISI 4340 steel, and nylon, adhering to detailed engineering drawings and dimensional tolerances. This project also contributes to the Harvey Mudd College tradition of student-made hammers.

    Each component was machined to tolerances within thousandths of an inch using a lathe and mill. Manufacturing techniques applied included drilling, tapping, heat treatment, and tempering — with the steel components undergoing heat treatment to achieve specified mechanical properties such as hardness, verified using an HRC Hardness Tester. Dimensional accuracy was continuously verified throughout the process using digital micrometers and GD&T principles.

title: Submersible Robot with Kp Control
text:
The finished submersible ROV.
  

  
    Background

    Underwater remotely operated vehicles provide a cost-effective solution for retrieving environmental data in aquatic settings. This project was motivated by the need to design and deploy a functional ROV capable of measuring temperature and pressure signals in lake environments.

    The goal was to develop a system that could reliably collect sensor data using the MCP9701 thermistor and MPX5700ASX pressure gauge, and process output voltages for analysis in LabVIEW. The ROV needed to be robust enough for real lake deployment while remaining buildable within the constraints of a course project.
  



To bring the system together, I assembled a PCB containing the MCP6002 OpAmp to condition and return output voltages from the sensors. Each circuit was carefully soldered and tested using an oscilloscope and DMM to verify signal integrity before deployment. The output voltages were then modeled and analyzed in LabVIEW, allowing us to interpret the sensor readings and validate the performance of the system in real aquatic conditions.
